Literal Interpretation

The Historical Context

Genesis 16 presents the account of Abram, Sarai, and Hagar, introducing the birth of Ishmael. The chapter takes place during a period of prolonged barrenness for Sarai, approximately ten years after Abram's arrival in Canaan (Gen 16:3). The narrative unfolds in three movements: Sarai's proposal and Hagar's conception (vv. 1-6), Hagar's flight and divine encounter (vv. 7-14), and the birth of Ishmael (vv. 15-16).

The opening verse establishes the central tension: "Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children" (Gen 16:1). In the ancient Near East, barrenness was considered a profound affliction, and the pressure to produce an heir was immense. The practice Sarai proposes—giving her maidservant to her husband to bear children on her behalf—was legally recognized in ancient Mesopotamian law codes, including the Code of Hammurabi.

Hagar the Egyptian

Hagar is identified as an Egyptian (Mitzrit), likely acquired during Abram and Sarai's sojourn in Egypt (Gen 12:10-20). Her name in Hebrew (Hagar) may be related to words meaning "flight" or "stranger," which proves thematically significant as the narrative unfolds. As a slave, Hagar occupied the lowest social position in the household, yet God would elevate her through a remarkable theophany.

Sarai's Proposal

"Go in unto my handmaid; it may be that I may obtain children by her" (Gen 16:2). Sarai's plan reflects both cultural custom and spiritual impatience. Rather than waiting for God's promised heir, she attempts to fulfill the divine promise through human means. St. Augustine, in his City of God, addresses this arrangement:

"Abraham is in no way to be branded as guilty concerning this concubine, for he used her for the begetting of progeny, not for the gratification of lust; and not to insult, but rather to obey his wife, who supposed it would be solace of her barrenness if she could make use of the fruitful womb of her handmaid to supply the defect of her own nature."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 25

Augustine further elaborates on Abram's conduct: "The handmaid is delivered to the husband by the wife for the sake of progeny, and is received by the husband for the sake of progeny, each seeking, not guilty excess, but natural fruit."

Hagar's Pride and Sarai's Affliction

Upon conceiving, "her mistress was despised in her eyes" (Gen 16:4). The Hebrew verb qalal (to be light, contemptible) indicates that Hagar began to look down upon Sarai. This reversal of social standing provoked Sarai's jealousy and harsh treatment. When Sarai "dealt hardly with her" (te'anneha—the same verb used for Egypt's affliction of Israel in Exodus 1:11-12), Hagar fled into the wilderness.

The Angel of the Lord

The phrase "the Angel of the Lord" (Malak YHWH) appears here for the first time in Scripture (Gen 16:7). This figure finds Hagar by a fountain of water in the wilderness, on the way to Shur—the road back toward Egypt. The Angel speaks with divine authority, using first-person divine pronouns: "I will multiply thy seed exceedingly" (Gen 16:10).

The early Church Fathers, including Justin Martyr, understood this Angel as a manifestation of the pre-incarnate Christ, the eternal Logos. Justin Martyr writes in his Dialogue with Trypho:

"He who is called God and appeared to the patriarchs is called both Angel and Lord, in order that from this you may understand Him to be minister to the Father."

St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter 58

Justin further explains: "God begot before all creatures a Beginning, a certain rational power proceeding from Himself, who is called by the Holy Spirit, now the Glory of the Lord, now the Son, again Wisdom, again an Angel, then God."

El Roi: The God Who Sees

Hagar's response to this theophany is remarkable. She names God El Roi—"The God who sees me" (Gen 16:13). The Hebrew El Roi (אֵל רֳאִי) combines El (God, mighty one) with Roi, derived from the verb ra'ah (to see). The Douay-Rheims renders verse 14: "Therefore she called that well, the well of him that liveth and seeth me."

This naming is extraordinary for several reasons: Hagar is the only person in all of Scripture to give a name to God. Not Eve, not Abraham, not Moses—but an Egyptian slave woman fleeing oppression. The name commemorates both God's watchful care over the afflicted and Hagar's astonishment at having survived a direct encounter with the divine: "Have I also here seen the back parts of him that seeth me?"

The Name Ishmael

The Angel commands Hagar to name her son Yishma'el—"God hears" (Gen 16:11). The name encapsulates God's compassionate attention to Hagar's affliction: "Because the Lord hath heard thy affliction." Though Ishmael would not be the child of promise, God heard Hagar's cry and responded with blessing. Ishmael would become the father of twelve princes and a great nation (Gen 17:20).

The Prophecy Concerning Ishmael

The Angel's prophecy describes Ishmael's character and destiny: "He shall be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him" (Gen 16:12). The Hebrew pere' adam ("wild donkey of a man") evokes the untamed freedom of the desert. St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, notes that Ishmael's descendants became the ancestors of the Arab peoples, making the ongoing conflict between Arab and Jew all the more tragic—for they are brothers sharing a common father in Abraham.

Hagar's Return and Ishmael's Birth

Instructed by the Angel to return and submit to Sarai, Hagar obeys. She bears a son to Abram, who names him Ishmael according to the divine instruction. Abram was eighty-six years old when Ishmael was born (Gen 16:16). For the next thirteen years, Ishmael would be Abram's only son, and it is reasonable to suppose that Abram cherished him deeply—which makes the later command regarding Isaac all the more poignant.

Allegorical Interpretation

The Two Covenants

St. Paul himself establishes the allegorical reading of Genesis 16 in his letter to the Galatians: "Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar" (Gal 4:24). This Pauline allegory became foundational for all subsequent patristic interpretation of the Hagar-Sarah narrative.

St. John Chrysostom expounds this allegory in his Homily 4 on Galatians:

"The mothers of those children, Sarah and Hagar; and what are they? Two covenants, two laws. For these women are two covenants; one from mount Sinai, bearing children unto bondage, which is Hagar."

St. John Chrysostom, Homily 4 on Galatians

Chrysostom further explains the geographical connection: "The bond-woman was called Hagar, and Hagar is the word for Mount Sinai in the language of that country. So that it is necessary that all who are born of the Old Covenant should be bondmen, for that mountain where the Old Covenant was delivered has a name in common with the bondwoman."

Hagar as the Old Covenant

In the allegorical framework, Hagar represents the Old Covenant given at Mount Sinai. Just as Hagar was a bondwoman, so the Mosaic Law, while holy and good in itself, could only produce spiritual bondage because it revealed sin without providing the grace to overcome it. Those who sought righteousness through the Law alone remained in slavery to sin and death.

Chrysostom elaborates: "Not only that she was in bondage and brought forth bondmen, but that this Covenant is so too, whereof the bondwoman was a type. For Jerusalem is adjacent to the mountain of the same name with the bondwoman, and in this mountain the Covenant was delivered."

Sarah as the New Covenant

Sarah, the free woman, represents the New Covenant of grace established in Christ. As St. Paul writes: "But Jerusalem that is above is free, which is the mother of us all" (Gal 4:26). The heavenly Jerusalem, the Church of Christ, is our mother—we are born not of the flesh but of the Spirit, not of law but of promise.

Chrysostom connects this to the Church: "But Jerusalem that is above is free—Sarah represents the heavenly Jerusalem and the Church of the Gentiles. Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are children of promise."

Ishmael and Isaac: Flesh and Spirit

The contrast between Ishmael and Isaac carries profound typological significance. Ishmael was born kata sarka—according to the flesh, through natural human effort. Isaac was born di' epangelias—through the promise, by divine intervention. This distinction prefigures the two ways of approaching God: through human works (symbolized by Ishmael) or through faith in divine grace (symbolized by Isaac).

As Paul states: "But as then he that was born after the flesh persecuted him that was born after the Spirit, even so it is now" (Gal 4:29). The persecution of Isaac by Ishmael foreshadows the persecution of the Church by those who reject the Gospel of grace.

The Angel of the Lord as the Pre-Incarnate Christ

The Church Fathers widely understood the Angel of the Lord who appeared to Hagar as a Christophany—an appearance of the pre-incarnate Son of God. Justin Martyr argues extensively in his Dialogue with Trypho that the divine figure who appeared to the patriarchs was the Logos, the Second Person of the Trinity.

"It is again written by Moses, my brethren, that He who is called God and appeared to the patriarchs is called both Angel and Lord, in order that from this you may understand Him to be minister to the Father."

St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter 58

This interpretation was shared by Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and St. Ambrose of Milan, among others. The Angel speaks with divine authority, makes promises only God can keep, and is identified by Hagar herself as God (El Roi). In this reading, Christ's ministry of mercy to the outcast and afflicted is prefigured in His appearance to the Egyptian slave woman in the wilderness.

The Two Jerusalems

The allegory extends to the contrast between two Jerusalems: the earthly Jerusalem, center of the old covenant worship, and the heavenly Jerusalem, the eternal city of God. Chrysostom explains this duality:

"There is an earthly Jerusalem, but this earthly Jerusalem typifies a heavenly Jerusalem: the former, with all her citizens, is in bondage; the latter is a free city, and all her inhabitants are free also."

St. John Chrysostom, Homily 4 on Galatians

The Wilderness as Place of Encounter

Hagar's encounter with God occurs in the wilderness, on the road to Shur. The wilderness is a recurring place of divine revelation in Scripture: Moses at the burning bush, Israel at Sinai, Elijah at Horeb, John the Baptist preparing the way. That God meets Hagar in this desolate place prefigures how Christ comes to those who are spiritually lost and wandering, offering living water in the desert of sin.

El Roi and the All-Seeing God

Hagar's naming of God as El Roi carries Christological significance. The God who sees is the same God who will take on flesh to dwell among us, to see and be seen, to know and be known. Christ is the visible image of the invisible God (Col 1:15), and His compassionate gaze extends to the lowliest and most marginalized. In Hagar's experience, we see a foreshadowing of Christ's ministry to the outcast, the foreigner, and the oppressed.

The Well of Living Water

The well where Hagar encounters God—Beer-lahai-roi, "the well of him that liveth and seeth me"—becomes a type of the living water that Christ offers. Just as Hagar found life-giving water in the wilderness, so Christ offers living water to all who thirst: "If any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink" (Jn 7:37). The Samaritan woman at the well echoes Hagar's experience—both are women of foreign origin who encounter the divine at a well and receive unexpected mercy.

Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

The Dangers of Impatience

The central moral lesson of Genesis 16 concerns the peril of attempting to fulfill God's promises through human scheming rather than patient faith. Sarai had received the promise of descendants through Abram, but after ten years of waiting, she devised her own solution. The consequences—jealousy, strife, and lasting enmity—demonstrate the bitter fruit of running ahead of God's timing.

St. Augustine, while defending Abraham's integrity, nonetheless observes that the plan originated from Sarai's impatience with her barrenness. The moral application is clear: when we attempt to accomplish God's purposes through worldly means, we often create problems that persist for generations. The faithful soul must learn to wait upon the Lord, trusting that His timing is perfect.

God's Care for the Afflicted

Despite the moral failures of Abram and Sarai, God shows remarkable compassion to Hagar—the victim caught in their scheme. Though a foreigner and a slave, she receives a personal visitation from the Angel of the Lord, a divine promise of blessing, and the honor of naming God. This demonstrates that God's mercy extends to all who suffer, regardless of social status or ethnic origin.

The moral lesson for Christians is profound: we are called to imitate God's preferential care for the vulnerable. Those who are marginalized, oppressed, or overlooked in human society are precious in God's sight. As James writes: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction" (Jas 1:27).

The Virtue of Humility

Hagar's downfall began when she despised her mistress upon conceiving. Pride transformed a blessing into a source of conflict. The moral teaching is timeless: when God blesses us—whether with children, success, or any good gift—we must guard against the pride that would lead us to look down upon others. Every good gift comes from God, and gratitude rather than arrogance should be our response.

Submission and Obedience

The Angel's command to Hagar is challenging: "Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands" (Gen 16:9). This instruction seems harsh to modern ears, but it carries a deeper spiritual meaning. Hagar is called to return not because slavery is good, but because flight from difficulty is rarely the path to blessing. Sometimes God calls us to endure hardship rather than escape it, trusting that He will work through our suffering.

This does not mean Christians must passively accept every injustice. Rather, the moral lesson is that we should not make major life decisions in the heat of anger or desperation. Hagar, fleeing impulsively into the wilderness, would have perished without divine intervention. The Angel's counsel brought her back to a situation that, while imperfect, would ultimately lead to blessing.

The God Who Sees

Hagar's confession—"Thou God seest me" (El Roi)—carries profound moral implications. We live always under the gaze of God. Nothing is hidden from His sight: our secret sins, our hidden motives, our unspoken thoughts. This awareness should inspire both holy fear and great comfort. We cannot hide from God, but neither can we be forgotten by Him.

As one reflection on El Roi states: "El Roi is the God who numbers the hairs on our heads and counts our every tear. He knows every detail of our circumstances. When we pray to El Roi, we are praying to the God who knows everything about us." The moral response to this truth is to live transparently before God, bringing all our struggles into the light of His presence.

Patience Through Trials

St. Basil the Great, though not commenting directly on this passage, teaches the broader principle that applies to Hagar's situation: "God does not leave His saints without trial, yet He bestows on them patient endurance." The trials of life—whether persecution, affliction, or prolonged waiting—are opportunities for the development of virtue. Hagar's wilderness experience, though painful, became the occasion for her deepest encounter with God.

The Consequences of Sin

Genesis 16 illustrates how sin creates rippling consequences that extend far beyond the original transgression. Sarai's impatience led to a plan that introduced lasting strife into the household. The enmity between the descendants of Isaac and Ishmael has continued for millennia. The moral warning is sobering: our choices matter, and their effects may persist long after we are gone. This should inspire us to seek God's will earnestly before acting, especially in matters of lasting consequence.

God's Faithfulness Despite Human Failure

Perhaps the most encouraging moral lesson is that God's purposes are not thwarted by human sin. Abram and Sarai's failure did not prevent God from fulfilling His promise. Though Isaac would come through Sarah, Ishmael too received blessing—a great nation would descend from him. God works redemptively even through our mistakes, weaving even our failures into His providential plan.

This truth should inspire both humility and hope. We should not presume upon God's mercy by sinning deliberately, but neither should we despair when we fail. The God who saw Hagar in the wilderness sees us in our struggles, and His grace is sufficient for every need.

Anagogical Interpretation

The Heavenly Jerusalem

The anagogical sense of Scripture directs our gaze toward the heavenly realities and the final consummation of all things. In Genesis 16, the contrast between Hagar and Sarah, developed fully in Galatians 4, points ultimately toward the heavenly Jerusalem that awaits the faithful. St. Paul writes: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all" (Gal 4:26).

St. John Chrysostom expounds on this heavenly city:

"But Jerusalem that is above is free, which is our mother. There is an earthly Jerusalem, but this earthly Jerusalem typifies a heavenly Jerusalem: the former, with all her citizens, is in bondage; the latter is a free city, and all her inhabitants are free also."

St. John Chrysostom, Homily 4 on Galatians

The heavenly Jerusalem described in Revelation 21-22 is the ultimate fulfillment of all that Sarah represents: freedom, promise, and eternal inheritance. The children of promise—all who are born of the Spirit through faith in Christ—are destined for this glorious city where God Himself dwells with His people.

Freedom from Bondage

The contrast between bondage and freedom in Genesis 16 anticipates the ultimate liberation from all slavery that awaits the redeemed. Hagar represents bondage to sin, death, and the law's curse—the condition of fallen humanity before Christ. Sarah represents the glorious liberty of the children of God, fully realized in the resurrection and the life of the world to come.

In heaven, there will be no more bondage of any kind: no slavery to sin, no subjection to death, no groaning under the weight of a fallen world. "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more" (Rev 21:4). The freedom that Sarah symbolizes finds its ultimate expression in the perfect liberty of eternal life.

The Vision of God

Hagar's wonder at having seen God and lived—"Have I also here seen the back parts of him that seeth me?"—points toward the beatific vision that is the crown of eternal life. In this present life, we see God only dimly, through veils and shadows. But in the life to come, "we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2).

The name El Roi—"The God who sees me"—will find its eschatological fulfillment when God's people see Him face to face. The mutual seeing between God and His creatures, which Hagar glimpsed momentarily in the wilderness, will become the eternal condition of the blessed. To be seen by God and to see God—this is the essence of heavenly beatitude.

The Well of Living Water

The well Beer-lahai-roi, where Hagar encountered the living God, prefigures the river of the water of life that flows through the heavenly city: "And he showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Rev 22:1). In this life, we drink from springs and wells that only partially satisfy our thirst. In eternity, we will drink freely from the source of all life.

The invitation extended to Hagar in the wilderness becomes the universal invitation of the eschaton: "And the Spirit and the bride say: Come. And he that heareth, let him say: Come. And he that thirsteth, let him come: and he that will, let him take the water of life, freely" (Rev 22:17).

The Multiplication of the Saints

The Angel's promise to Hagar—"I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude" (Gen 16:10)—echoes the promise given to Abraham and points toward the innumerable company of the redeemed. In John's vision of heaven, he beholds "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb" (Rev 7:9).

This eschatological gathering includes not only the children of Isaac but representatives from every nation—Gentiles who, like Hagar the Egyptian, have received God's mercy and been incorporated into His people. The barriers of ethnicity, social status, and national origin that divided humanity in Genesis will be abolished in the heavenly kingdom.

The Inheritance of the Saints

Chrysostom draws out the eschatological implications of Paul's allegory: "Cast out the handmaid and her son: for the son of the handmaid shall not inherit with the son of the freewoman" (Gal 4:30). The inheritance promised to Abraham's seed—ultimately, eternal life in the presence of God—belongs to the children of promise. Those who seek to inherit by works of the law, apart from faith in Christ, will find themselves excluded.

The eternal inheritance is described throughout the New Testament: an incorruptible crown, treasures in heaven, the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world. This inheritance is reserved for those who, like Isaac, are born not of the flesh but of the Spirit—regenerated by grace through faith in Christ.

The Final Separation

The separation of Ishmael from Isaac's household foreshadows the final separation that will occur at the last judgment. As Jesus teaches in the parable of the wheat and tares, the children of the kingdom and the children of the wicked one grow together until the harvest. Then comes the separation: the wheat gathered into the barn, the tares bound for burning.

This sobering reality underscores the importance of being children of promise rather than children of the flesh—of being born again by the Spirit rather than trusting in natural descent or human effort. The time of mixture will end, and each will receive according to what has been done.

Already and Not Yet

The freedom that Sarah represents is both a present reality and a future hope. Through baptism and faith, believers already participate in the New Covenant and are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem. Yet the fullness of that freedom awaits the resurrection, when our bodies will be glorified and creation itself will be liberated from its bondage to decay.

We live in the tension between the "already" of our spiritual adoption and the "not yet" of our full glorification. Like Hagar, we are on a journey—not fleeing into the wilderness, but traveling toward the celestial city. And like Hagar, we are sustained on the way by the God who sees us and provides wells of living water in our pilgrimage.

The Eternal Sabbath

The eschatological vision of Scripture culminates in eternal rest—the heavenly Sabbath where all labor, strife, and sorrow cease. The conflict between Sarai and Hagar, the enmity between their descendants, the long history of human discord—all will be swallowed up in the peace of God's eternal kingdom. "There remaineth therefore a day of rest for the people of God" (Heb 4:9). This rest, prefigured in the seventh day of creation, awaits all who persevere in faith to the end.
